young.html: Karl Marx spent years in a great London library, reading reports about factories, money and work, and writing a giant book called Capital. He wanted to answer a question: where do the profits of a business come from?

Marx's answer was that profits come from the workers. He said workers make more value in a day than they are paid for, and the owner keeps the extra. Most economists since then have disagreed and explain wages and profits in other ways, but his book made many people pay attention to how hard factory work was in the 1800s, when people, even children, often worked twelve hours or more.

full.html: Marx (1818–1883), with Engels the co-author of the Communist Manifesto, settled in London in 1849 as a refugee. Supported largely by Engels, he worked for years in the reading room of the British Museum on a critique of the economists. Volume 1 of Capital: A Critique of Political Economy appeared in Hamburg in 1867; Engels assembled Volumes 2 and 3 from Marx's manuscripts after his death. The English translation by Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling, edited by Engels, came out in 1887.

full.text: The wealth of those societies in which the capitalist mode of production prevails, presents itself as "an immense accumulation of commodities," its unit being a single commodity. Our investigation must therefore begin with the analysis of a commodity.

full.html: A commodity has a use value (what it is good for) and an exchange value (what it trades for). Following the classical economists Adam Smith and David Ricardo, Marx holds a labor theory of value: what gives goods their exchange value is the labor time socially necessary to make them.

full.text: The simplest form of the circulation of commodities is C—M—C, the transformation of commodities into money, and the change of the money back again into commodities; or selling in order to buy. But alongside of this form we find another specifically different form: M—C—M, the transformation of money into commodities, and the change of commodities back again into money; or buying in order to sell.
full.author: Marx
full.ed: first American edition, Charles H. Kerr, Chicago

full.html: Where does the extra in M–C–M′ come from, if goods trade at their value? Marx's answer: the worker sells his labor power, his capacity to work, for a wage that covers what he needs to live. But in a working day he can produce more value than that wage. The difference Marx calls surplus value, the source, in his theory, of profit.

full.html: The long middle of Volume 1 uses the reports of British factory inspectors to describe working conditions in the 1860s: very long hours, child labor, dangerous machines. Marx describes the fight over the Factory Acts, which limited hours, as a struggle over surplus value. Historians still value these chapters as a record of industrial life.

In the 1870s William Stanley Jevons, Carl Menger and Léon Walras independently developed marginal utility: the value of a thing depends on how useful one more unit is to people, not on the labor it took. Most economists since then reject the labor theory of value, and with it Marx's account of profit, explaining wages and profits instead by supply and demand for labor and capital, risk, and the value each adds. Critics such as Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk (1896) pointed to contradictions between Volumes 1 and 3. Marx's predictions that profits would fall and workers grow poorer did not come true in industrial countries. Marxist economists have offered replies, and the book remains much studied in the history of economic thought, sociology and history.

Treating Capital's theory of value as settled economics. It is a 19th-century theory, built on Ricardo, that most economists have replaced; its descriptions of 1860s factories are another matter, and are widely accepted.

items: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (earlier on this ladder) is the book Marx answers most often: the division of labor, wages, profit and the market.
Hegel: Marx said Hegel's method stood on its head and had to be "turned right side up," with material life first.
Aristotle's Politics had already distinguished using a thing from trading it, and questioned money made from money; Marx cites him.
Dickens, later in this era, shows the same London of debt, poverty and grinding work in fiction.
